newsitem.title: FRANCE: Strikes disrupt French rail service in some areas.
newsitem.headline: Strikes disrupt French rail service in some areas.

text.p: Work stoppages by railway employees worried over possible job losses disrupted regional service in southwest France for a second consecutive day on Tuesday, the SNCF national rail authority said.
Just one train in five was running on the main routes in the region though high-speed TGV passenger trains were unaffected by the stoppages, SNCF officials said.
Traffic was also cut disrupted early on Tuesday around Nantes in orthwestern France, when hooded workers climbed onto the tracks to block some regional trains, Europe 1 radio reported.

The partial stoppages followed a threat by the two most powerful SNCF unions on Monday to call a nationwide strike on October 17 to coincide with a nationwide strike appeal by powerful civil service unions.

The Communist-led CGT union said after a meeting between employee representatives and SNCF management that it was weighing a "day of action" on October 17 in protest at proposed staff cuts and other worries about the SNCF's future.

Rail workers spearheaded a crippling 24-day strike and wider unrest late last year when the centre-right government of Prime Minister Alain Juppe proposed ending their early pension rights -- proposals which have since been scrapped.

The gripe this time, over programmed cuts in staffing levels and a modernisation plan which involves taking huge debts off the SNCF's hands, is harder to measure in terms of its potential to mobilise the railworkers themselves or wider public support.
The CGT said in a statement that the employee representatives had voted overwhelmingly against a proposed modernisation plan for the SNCF "in its current form".

The plan commits the government to take 125 billion French francs ($24.40 billion) of debt off the loss-making SNCF's hands by spinning it off into another state company which would also become owner of the track and other infrastructure.
Unions fear the plan could open the way to additional staff cuts or a possible privatisation of the SNCF if political imperatives were to change in the future.
A rail strike on October 17 would coincide with strike calls by the seven main civil service unions to protest against plans to cut 6,000 jobs next year and to press for a pay increase.
